title: Capacity contract and eviction policy discussion
summary: Intro discovery on dedicated capacity: tuning reservation size, isolation/tenant quarantine, eviction behavior during bursts, and SSO/KMS compliance. Customer wants firm eviction guarantees and a burst fallback that preserves P95 latency for critical routes. Agreed to run a 2-week pilot with synthetic burst tests and share security docs.
topics: tenant isolation models (hard vs soft tenancy)
action_items: Alex Chen: Send pilot agreement template + pricing estimate by 2027-09-09
Samira Kapoor: Share dedicated topology diagram and eviction policy doc (internal RFC) by 2027-09-10
Priya Nair: Provide list of critical API routes and target P95 latency by 2027-09-12
Diego Ramos: Grant limited access to performance telemetry for test cluster by 2027-09-14
next_steps: Schedule pilot kickoff (2 week window) — target 2027-09-15 start
Redwood to run synthetic burst and warm-pool tests and share results
Customer to review security whitepaper and confirm KMS/HSM requirements
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-09-07
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Samira Kapoor (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Arborwell CTO), Diego Ramos (Infra Lead), Hannah Cole (Head of Security), Marcus Yoon (Product)

Auto-generated summary (may be incomplete): Discussed dedicated capacity sizing, isolation guarantees, eviction behavior, and compliance hooks. Customer asked for firm fallback behavior and pilot.

[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, appreciate you carving out time. quick round-robin — from Redwood samira and jordan are with me, we'll talk infra and runbooks. Priya, wanna kick off with your priorities?
[00:18] Priya Nair: Sure yeah thanks Alex. Our big thing is throughput predictability — we've got three high-volume routes that power the live product. we can't have momentary thrash that spikes cost or drops p95 beyond 300ms. We're evaluating hosted vs dedicated vs private, but for now focusing on dedicated reservation because of data residency and latency guarantees.
[00:42] Diego Ramos: To add, our infra team needs a clear eviction behavior. If you preempt warm nodes during a spike what exactly happens to the in-flight requests, and do we get telemetry to correlate with traces?
[01:01] Samira Kapoor: Totally. So our dedicated pools support configurable eviction windows. there's soft eviction which attempts to drain KV cache and finish in-flight, and hard eviction which is immediate with fallback routing. both have tradeoffs for latency and cost.
[01:20] Hannah Cole: And from security, we need auditability around any failover. if requests shift between dedicated and hosted, we need logs and KMS keys usage records, ideally HSM-backed and exported to your SIEM. SOC2 is a must.
[01:39] Jordan Lee: Quick clarification — when you say 'shift', are you imagining automatic routing to a hosted model variant or to an alternate dedicated warm pool?
[01:50] Priya Nair: Prefer hosted variant for non-PII routes, dedicated for PII. we want controls to pin PII to private/dedicated and have automatic fallback only for non-PII.
[02:06] Alex Chen: That maps to our routing policy features — you can tag routes and apply policy that routes by data-sensitivity attribute. we can also do canary steps so each fallback is observable.
[02:22] Diego Ramos: About prewarming — how aggressive is your warm pool? we see a lot of headroom in the morning spike and then flatline. we need to size reserve such that cost isn't crazy but tail latency is okay.
[02:36] Samira Kapoor: We recommend sizing reserved capacity for steady-state plus 20-30% buffer, then rely on a warm pool for burst. warm pool prewarm times depend on model size and quantization — for our 13B q4 models it's roughly 18-35 seconds to reach full KV capacity in most regions, maybe longer with cold disk loads.
[02:58] Marcus Yoon: 18-35s could be painful for live chat; any mitigations?
[03:04] Samira Kapoor: Two levers — prefix caching and synthetic preheating. We can keep a small set of cached prefixes for the critical endpoints so first token latency reduces. also continuous small-batch traffic from health pingers reduces cold start frequency.
[03:20] Priya Nair: That sounds good. On eviction policy specifics, can you walk us through a scenario where capacity is exhausted midday and a priority tenant needs to remain?
[03:33] Samira Kapoor: Sure so we have tenant priority tiers. in hard tenancy, you'd get dedicated physical isolation — no eviction except by explicit admin action. in soft tenancy you have shared nodes with tenant fencing and preemption tiers. If capacity is exhausted, the scheduler will first attempt to scale within reserved headroom, then pull from warm pool; if still insufficient, it will preempt lower-priority tenants based on policy. preempted tenants will be flagged and routed to a compatible hosted variant unless pinned.
[04:05] Diego Ramos: Is that preemption deterministic? we need reproducible behaviour for audits.
[04:11] Jordan Lee: It's policy-driven — deterministic given the same active set and policy weights, but not strictly time-deterministic because of race windows. we log each decision and a replayable event stream for auditability.
[04:26] Hannah Cole: Good. And KMS — we need envelope encryption and customer-managed keys. what are your supported integrations?
[04:34] Alex Chen: We support AWS KMS, GCP KMS, Azure Key Vault, and HSM integrations via our private deployment. for hosted, we can do envelope encryption with BYOK (bring-your-own-key) where you retain control. logs show key usage events.
[04:50] Hannah Cole: For SOC2 audit we'll need a runbook for key rotation and proof we never persist plaintext in the control plane.
[04:57] Samira Kapoor: We'll share our security whitepaper and an implementation guide. we'll also map the control plane role and explain where plaintext is zeroed out.
[05:08] Priya Nair: On the pilot, what exactly will be measured? Diego is going to want throughput vs p95 under synthetic bursts.
[05:15] Diego Ramos: yes we want step loads — add 50% traffic for 10 minutes then ramp to 300% for 2 minutes every hour for two days, to simulate flash promotions. we need end-to-end telemetry and KV cache hit rates.
[05:33] Samira Kapoor: we can run that in a mirrored staging environment in our dedicated cluster. we'll instrument request tracing and kv hit/miss, and we can produce a report: p50/p95/p99, eviction events, fallback counts, and token cost deltas.
[05:47] Marcus Yoon: Cost deltas are key. show us token/cost when using prefix cache vs not.
[05:54] Alex Chen: We'll include cost modeling for typical prompts. also we'll show quantization tradeoffs if you need lower memory footprint — that can reduce prewarm time.
[06:04] Priya Nair: About SLAs — you mentioned SLO tiers previously, what realistic SLO can Redwood guarantee for dedicated?
[06:12] Jordan Lee: For dedicated reserved pools with standard SLAs we target 99.9% availability at the node level and P95 latency SLOs depending on model and request size — we'll baseline during the pilot. the SLA will exclude customer-induced misconfiguration and large-scale infra provider outages.
[06:29] Diego Ramos: And about pricing — what is the reservation commitment cadence, monthly or annual? is there a tier for burst credits?
[06:36] Alex Chen: We offer monthly and annual commitments. annual gives better unit pricing. we also offer a burst credit buffer as an add-on which guarantees a fixed burst capacity for short windows; alternatively you can use on-demand hosted fallback which bills per token.
[06:51] Priya Nair: We prefer predictable billing; burst credits sound interesting. can you lock a burst pool to a customer so others can't consume it?
[06:59] Samira Kapoor: Yes, that would be a dedicated hotpool — you pay for reserved burst capacity that is isolated. it's more expensive but gives hard guarantees.
[07:10] Diego Ramos: Any constraints around preemption when hotpool is reserved? we don't want silent eviction when they say reserved.
[07:16] Jordan Lee: If you reserve a hotpool it's excluded from eviction, it's hard tenancy. only manual admin actions or contract-level reductions will evict those nodes.
[07:25] Priya Nair: Okay, good. Now on observability — can we ingest Redwood traces into our Datadog and our internal tracing?
[07:33] Alex Chen: yes we have exporters for Datadog and Zipkin/OpenTelemetry. we can also push aggregated metrics to customers' cloud monitoring via pushgateway.
[07:44] Hannah Cole: For compliance we also need detailed audit logs of route changes and fallbacks with user IDs.
[07:51] Samira Kapoor: We can include route-change audit logs and keep them in an append-only store for the retention window you choose—longer retention is an add-on.
[07:59] Diego Ramos: A technical question — how do you handle KV cache warmup when a tenant is moved to a different node? is there a serialization step that causes head-of-line blocking?
[08:09] Jordan Lee: We stream KV state incrementally; initial requests might have slightly more RTT until the cache ramps. to avoid head-of-line blocking we do asynchronous KV fetch with a fallback to a slimmer model path and stitch results once KV is available. it's not perfect but reduces blocking.
[08:27] Priya Nair: That asynchronous approach may add complexity for our client SDKs. can we get a sample SDK pattern to handle partial responses?
[08:35] Alex Chen: yes, we'll include SDK best-practices for optimistic reads and stitch on client.
[08:41] Marcus Yoon: On the timeline — if we sign a pilot mid-September what is a realistic production on-ramp?
[08:48] Samira Kapoor: If pilot goes well, a 6-8 week onramp to production is typical for dedicated: contract, provisioning, integration for KMS and SSO, and load tests. but depends on complexity of PII pinning and any private/VPC needs.
[09:02] Priya Nair: Security question — for private deployment, do you run the control plane in our VPC or do we manage the control plane entirely?
[09:11] Alex Chen: For private we offer two modes: SaaS control plane with customer-managed network peering and proxy, or full-on-prem control plane where you host the control plane components. Both can integrate with your KMS/HSM.
[09:24] Hannah Cole: We might require a full private control plane for PHI workloads. that'll be a separate talk but good to know it's an option.
[09:33] Diego Ramos: One more thing — can you show us a concrete eviction trace? a timeline of an eviction event with associated metrics so we can simulate failure modes.
[09:43] Jordan Lee: Absolutely, we have recent audit traces and we can anonymize them. we'll pull a sample and annotate what the scheduler did.
[09:52] Priya Nair: Perfect. Any competitor switch concerns? we looked at AtlasEdge and NimbusAI, both offer something similar but we like Redwood's observability model. question is long-term cost.
[10:05] Alex Chen: we can provide a cost projection comparing dedicated with warm pools + reserved burst vs hosted-only. we'll put the unit token costs and node amortization in a spreadsheet.
[10:15] Marcus Yoon: ok good.
[10:18] -- brief pause as folks check links --
[10:31] Samira Kapoor: Quick note on benchmarking — please share representative prompts and request sizes. even a synthetic distribution helps us choose model variant and quantization.
[10:40] Diego Ramos: we'll share payload sizes and a sample of top 50 prompts.
[10:45] Priya Nair: and we'll flag which routes are PII.
[10:48] Alex Chen: Great. For the pilot acceptance criteria, can we propose: 1) p95 under 300ms for critical routes during 90% of synthetic bursts, 2) no unplanned eviction of pinned PII tenants, 3) audit logs produced and shared.
[11:05] Priya Nair: That seems fair. Diego will internalize details but yes.
[11:09] Hannah Cole: Add requirement for KMS proof and key rotation policy docs.
[11:13] Alex Chen: Noted.
[11:17] Jordan Lee: We'll also attach a sample runbook for warm-pool troubleshooting.
[11:22] Marcus Yoon: If pilot fails to meet p95 on critical routes, what's remediation path? rollback to hosted?
[11:29] Samira Kapoor: We will either tweak warm-pool sizing, adjust prefix cache, or fall back to hosted variant until we can address the issue. we'll document the remediation path in the pilot runbook.
[11:41] Priya Nair: Ok. Anything else from the customer side?
[11:44] Diego Ramos: Not right now. I'll follow up with the telemetry access.
[11:48] Hannah Cole: I'll review the security docs once you share.
[11:51] Alex Chen: Great. quick recap of next steps: we'll send pilot agreement and pricing, eviction policy RFC, sample audit trace, and runbook. customer will share test prompts, critical route list, and telemetry access.
[12:06] Priya Nair: Thanks everyone. Looking forward to the kickoff.
[12:09] Alex Chen: Thanks, we'll follow up by email. bye.

Meeting end.
